intro: Slow, dropping WiFi is usually an **interference** problem, not a speed-plan problem. Neighboring routers piled onto the same channel fight for the same airtime. This guide tells you which channels to pick on **2.4 GHz** and **5 GHz** so your network stops stepping on its neighbors — and theirs stop stepping on you.
keyTakeaway: On **2.4 GHz** only three channels don't overlap: **1, 6 and 11** — pick one and stick to it. On **5 GHz** you have many more non-overlapping channels, so let the router auto-select (DFS channels avoid radar). When in doubt, use a WiFi analyzer app to see which channel your neighbors are crowding, and choose the emptiest one.

explanation:
## Why 2.4 GHz only has three good channels

The 2.4 GHz band has 11–13 numbered channels (region-dependent), but each one is ~20–22 MHz wide while the channels are spaced only 5 MHz apart. That means adjacent channels **overlap and bleed into each other**. Only **1, 6 and 11** are far enough apart not to overlap. Setting your router to channel 3 or 9 doesn't give you private spectrum — it just smears interference across two of the clean channels. Pick 1, 6, or 11 and choose whichever your neighbors use least.

## 5 GHz: more room, two catches

The 5 GHz band offers far more non-overlapping channels (the exact count depends on your country's regulations), so congestion is rarely the problem it is on 2.4 GHz. Two things to know:

- **DFS channels** (Dynamic Frequency Selection) share spectrum with weather and military radar. Routers may use them, but must vacate instantly if radar is detected — which can cause a brief drop. Most routers handle this automatically.
- **Channel width** trades speed for cleanliness. 80 MHz or 160 MHz channels are faster but swallow several channels at once, raising the odds of overlap in a crowded building. In an apartment, 40 MHz is often more stable than 80 MHz.

## 2.4 vs 5 GHz: which band for what

2.4 GHz travels farther and through walls better, so it's the band for far rooms and old smart-home gadgets. 5 GHz is faster with much less interference but shorter range — ideal for streaming and gaming near the router. Modern routers broadcast both at once, often under one name ("band steering"), letting each device pick the better band.

## How to actually choose

1. Install a WiFi analyzer app (e.g. on Android or a desktop tool) and walk around your home.
2. On 2.4 GHz, see whether 1, 6, or 11 is least crowded — set your router to that one manually.
3. On 5 GHz, leave the router on **auto** unless you see a specific congested channel.
4. Re-check after any new neighbors move in; the radio environment changes over time.

For enterprise deployments or regulatory questions, consult a network specialist — channel availability and DFS rules vary by country.

faq.q: Why are channels 1, 6, and 11 recommended for 2.4 GHz?
faq.a: These are the only three non-overlapping channels in the 2.4 GHz band. Using other channels will cause interference with neighboring networks and reduce performance.

faq.q: How many channels does 5 GHz WiFi have?
faq.a: The 5 GHz band supports 19 or more non-overlapping channels depending on your region, offering much more flexibility than 2.4 GHz and better performance in congested areas.
DFS allows WiFi routers to detect and automatically avoid radar signals on 5 GHz channels. This is required by law in many countries and regions.

faq.q: Should I use 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz?
faq.a: Use 2.4 GHz for better range and compatibility with older devices. Use 5 GHz for faster speeds and less interference. Modern routers support both bands simultaneously for optimal performance.

160 MHz channel width offers faster speeds but uses more spectrum, reduces the number of available channels, and can cause more interference. Use only if you have adequate space and few neighboring networks.
